question:
Tinkerdeck's window is cluttered: roughly ten ungrouped top-bar controls, up to six stacked parts in an app view and up to five banners all compete for attention, so a first-time user cannot see what matters. This feature is a tidy-up, not a redesign: the same screens, panels, dialogs, footer and separate editor view stay, but top-bar controls are grouped, advanced controls are hidden until needed, optional parts start hidden or collapsed and can be hidden again on demand, the last layout is remembered between sessions, VS Code-style shortcuts are added, and a command palette keeps every hidden action reachable by name. A written, inspected tidy-up plan is produced first. The requirements are mostly window (React) work; remembering the layout (R9) is stored with the core's existing saved settings so it survives a restart, and R10 adds new front-end npm dependencies that the plan must verify against React 18.3 and the Tauri webview.

What will be built:

1. R1: Before any window code changes, produce a tidy-up plan that names every current screen, panel, dialog, footer element,…
2. R2: Keep every current screen, panel, dialog, the footer and the separate editor view; the tidy-up changes only how control…
3. R3: Group related top-bar controls into named groups with a stated purpose, keep Shell and Theme directly reachable without…
4. R4: Add VS Code-style keyboard shortcuts while keeping the existing app shortcuts: Ctrl+B toggles the sidebar, F5 refreshes…
5. R5: Hide parts the user is not working on instead of keeping them on screen: collapse or lazy-load the git tools and the co…
6. R6: Keep the footer, and make its toggle behave the same as the sidebar's Ctrl+B toggle so the two stay in step.

…and 4 more (the full list is in the requirements file).

These may pull against each other (if you already know which matters more, say so):

1. R5 and R9: R5 wants the git tools and the console hidden until the user asks for them, while R9 restores the last layout. A user who left the git drawer and two consoles open would see them reopen at startup, so the plan must say whether restoring the last layout outranks starting with the calm minimal view.
2. R3 and R9: R3 hides advanced top-bar controls so a first-time user sees fewer of them, while R9 restores a returning user's layout. If an existing user had left those advanced controls visible, restoring the layout shows them again, so the plan must say which wins for a returning user.
3. R2 and R10: R2 says keep the existing hand-built menus and roughly eight dialogs, while R10 prefers package-backed menus and dialogs. Swapping them for a library's versions gains focus handling but risks becoming the replacement R2 rules out, so the plan must decide whether a package-backed dialog with the same content and actions still counts as the same dialog.

Assumed for you (tell me if any is wrong):

1. The remembered layout is a small fixed set of open/collapsed/hidden flags for the optional parts the plan names, stored with the app's existing saved settings…
2. The default calm view hides the git tools and the console until asked; folder-lock, job-warning, error and available-update signals stay visible or noticeable…

Not included:

• Making UI code changes before the tidy-up plan has been written, checked against the running app and agreed.
• Redesigning or replacing existing screens, views, panels, dialogs, the footer or the navigation flow.
• Embedding the editor inside the app view; it stays a separate full view.
• Changing what existing functions do; only where they live, how they are grouped, whether they show by default, how they are hidden, whether their state is reme…

Are these right? Approve them, or tell me in your own words what to change.

What you asked for needs 10 requirements, which is more than DevTeam can build in one run: plans that need more than about 20 parts have often not finished in earlier runs (they stall, and you wait many hours for nothing). Instead DevTeam proposes 2 revisions. It builds one revision at a time, as a feature of its own, and stops at the end of each so you can test it. If you are happy it starts the next; if not, you tell it in plain words what to change. Everything happens on this one branch, and nothing is merged until the end.
optionLabel: Build it in revisions, starting with revision 1

optionLabel: Keep waiting for a long time

question:
Before anything is built, DevTeam found instructions that cannot all be followed. Think of two people, Alice and Bob, who were each told something different.
Alice is R3, what you asked for. Bob is the house rule USR-001. R3 regroups the top-bar controls into named groups, and the design does this by hand-building TopBar, UtilitiesMenu, AppFooter and a command palette, explicitly leaving the jattac packages installed 'in preference of any other components' for a later revision; a UtilitiesMenu performs the same function as jattac.libs.web.overflow-menu and the new buttons the same function as zest-button.
Alice is R5, what you asked for. Bob is the design (design). R5 requires dialogs that are not shown to be lazy-loaded so the initial view does not carry them; the design keeps UpdateDialog in the eager module purely because it shares a file with the always-needed banner, which is a co-location convenience, not a technical necessity (the module can be split).
Alice is R3, what you asked for. Bob is the design (design). The design's scope and impact include src/App.module.css, which is an old area, and it says the header rules are moved out of it. No requirement needs the existing header rules removed: the new TopBar.module.css can carry the new rules while the old file is left alone, so this is a reorganisation of an old file for convenience. The design states no technical reason why new code plus an adapter in features/ cannot meet R3 without touching the old stylesheet.
Nothing done so far is thrown away. How should it be settled?
optionLabel: Keep the requirement, and relax USR-001, TEST-001 for this feature

Alice is R9, what you asked for. Bob is an earlier accepted requirement (20261125-153618:R5). R9 restores an app's saved open git drawer and console when that app is opened, which makes the earlier R5 promise that opening an app shows neither the git tools nor the console until the user asks untrue; both requirements cannot hold at once, so the builder has to say which wins.
Alice is R8, what you asked for. Bob is the design (design). R8 says every optional part that can be opened also has a control that hides it again, but the design disables the console's only hide control when the console is the only workspace, so a console on screen in that case cannot be hidden and the design's own Reset layout result cannot be reached.
Alice is R7, what you asked for. Bob is the design (design). R7 requires the command palette to list every app action, but the design deliberately keeps the editor's own file commands (Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+N new file) off the palette, so the stated 'every action' acceptance cannot pass even though the palette opens while the editor is focused.
Nothing done so far is thrown away. How should it be settled?

All work is in the window (React); the saved layout uses the window's existing local preference store, so no Rust command, permission or config format changes.

question: May the design add Reuse the existing sidebar preference instead of a new layout record? R9 only needs the window-level sidebar state, and the sidebar's collapsed flag is already saved under td.sidebarCollapsed with a safe fallback, so keeping that key avoids a migration and makes it impossible to restore an app's git drawer or console at startup.
answer: Allowed by engine: an enabling addition that touches nothing sensitive
